newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: APEC to signal current currency levels acceptable.
newsitem.headline: APEC to signal current currency levels acceptable.

text.p: Asia-Pacific finance ministers on Sunday were poised to signal that current foreign exchange rates in the region were at acceptable levels, APEC officials said.

The ministers of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum also appeared ready to take the grouping into a new era of policy coordination by declaring that their financial markets were interdependent.

APEC delegates said the currency views and policy coordination were top items in the communique, which the ministers planned to issue later on Sunday at the end of their weekend meeting at this luxury resort.
The communique will state that major currency misalignments, which could have negative effects on the member countries' trade and economic situations, have been corrected, delegates said.

That is something the powerful Group of Seven (G7) industrialised nations have been saying, as the communique is expected to specifically note, and could be seen as an endorsement of exchange rates roughly around current levels.
Only hours before the ministers were to give their final news conference, Malaysian Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim said the APEC'S views on exchange rates need to be heard.
APEC's currency comments were partly in response to the G7, Anwar said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television.
"We think that any intervention or various expressions on the issue should take into consideration all the international community, and not be confined to the established group," Anwar said.

He said APEC talking about exchange rates is not a question of agressiveness, but "a question of gaining confidence and realising the need to have an effective mechanism of our own and not be susceptible to unpredictable developments."

On policy coordination, APEC will note that interdependence of member economies and financial markets is deepening, and will agree to strengthen coordination in order to make their economies more resilient to shocks from events outside the region, Japanese officials said.
Other sources said the communique would also call for the completion by the end of the year of worldwide negotiations on liberalising financial services.
Ministers will also endorse proposals to help attract more than $1 trillion for Asian infrastructure development and to promote a freer flow of capital.

The fund flow proposals centre around more uniform regulation among members, transparency and availability of information, easing the ability to invest internationally and liberalising financial markets.

On Saturday, an advisory group of APEC private financiers listed a series of concrete steps they wanted member governments to take -- from the establishment of regional information centres on financing needs to creation of bond-rating agencies.
"Very high-level business people gave their recommendations on how the public and private sectors should cooperate to sustain the flow of money into the region," one Japanese official said.

APEC comprises Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand and the United States.
